candidates.description: Natural scenes are perceived despite attention being directed to another task and therefore do not produce inattentional blindness.
candidates.citation_sentence: It has previously been claimed that inattentional blindness does not occur for natural scenes [17].
candidates.notes: Experiment 1a tested this claim using a more demanding multiple-object-tracking task and found substantial inattentional blindness.

candidates.original_title: Why does natural scene categorization require little attention? Exploring attentional requirements for natural and synthetic stimuli
candidates.description: Natural-scene perception is unaffected by dual-task interference and requires little or no attention.
candidates.citation_sentence: Previous studies have found that scene perception is unaffected by dual-task interference [8][16][29].
candidates.notes: Experiment 2 found no interference at slow tracking speed but significant interference at fast tracking speed.

candidates.original_title: Why does natural scene categorization require little attention? Exploring attentional requirements for natural and synthetic stimuli
candidates.description: Natural-scene perception, including detection and categorization of scene contents, is largely unaffected by a demanding concurrent task.
candidates.citation_sentence: Given that we followed previous studies in using a task that required the detection and classification of animals and vehicles within a scene, the difference in results between the current study and previous studies [16][29][35] cannot be attributed to a difference in the task used to assess scene perception.
candidates.notes: Experiment 3 found dual-task costs for both five-category scene classification and animal-vehicle classification, but the replication used a demanding RSVP task and therefore provides conditional rather than unqualified evidence.

candidates.description: Animals and other semantic information in natural scenes can be detected and categorized rapidly with minimal attention.
